newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: OPINION COLUMN - Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala.
newsitem.headline: OPINION COLUMN - Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala.

text.p: Following are excerpts from an interview given by Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala, president of Ayala Corp, to Reuters.
--------------- ON THE ECONOMY:

We have had positive GNP growth for about five years now in a row. In addition to that you have a very stable macroeconomic environment. There has been single-digit inflation for quite a few years now and very strong foreign exchange reserves which have been increasing every year. And the general liberalisation and privatisation policy of the government is the kind of free market economics that business groups like ourselves like.
Add to that the kind of political stability that President Ramos has brought in during his term and it's just a wonderful combination and a wonderful framework in which to do business.

I think it's important to understand that framework first. (It) has been a framework that has been consistent for some years now. Within that there have been many opportunities for corporations to then work within that framework -- be they at entrepreneurial levels, small-scale levels or larger levels.

I'd like to add as a further element to this the fact that the country has attracted a lot of attention in recent years. It's made our capital market a very exciting place. And mix that with the fact that emerging markets as a whole are of great interest ot the global financial markets - it's been very easy for the Philippines to be recognised and capital has become something that is available. Actually I'm of the belief that capital is no longer a scarce resource that it used to be in the past. It's really managerial resources and opportunities that are the drivers in this kind of environment.
THE ROAD AHEAD

We've had a very difficult 1980s so in relative terms we are all very excited by what we see. But it is very important to understand that the macroeconomic environment still has a long way to go. We have tremendous needs in infrastructure. I think the current administration has taken great strides in privatising and liberalising and encouraging the private sector to take up the public sector slack. But that having been said, there is still a great amount that needs to be done in terms of roads, railways. ports -- in basic facilities that will enable the country to keep growing at this pace.
MANAGERIAL REQUIREMENTS

From a managerial point of view, countries like the Philippines are by their nature somewhat imperfect. We don't have smooth-working bureaucracies and while we have moved forward a great deal there is still a lot that needs to be done. So, you have to be able to work within a somewhat uncertain environment. Luckily for us, the current government is giving us a consistency in policies which has not always been there in the past.

In the current environment, managers have to be very resourceful, you have to be very entrepreneurial -- there are many opportunities opening up. One has to have one's ears very close to the ground. The business variables are different once you get into some of these projects -- you have to be quite attuned to the kind of risks involved. But if you feel you can manage all these things, then there are some very exciting opportunities and quite large in scale. It's quite exciting not only by local standards but certainly by global standards.
THE AYALA GROUP IN THE BOOMING PHILIPPINES

We're doing a lot better in this environment than we ever have done in the past because when a country grows the way the Philippines has been growing there's room for everyone. One must never be scared about new entrants. As long as you keep your standards high, keep your world-class standards in place, have a very, very professional outlook in what you do, bring first class partners (which is something we've always been very excited about), everything is there to participate in.

What I would like to bring is a certain urgency to the way we (Ayala) do things -- really move a lot quicker to take advantage of some of the opportunities that are opening up around us. We have traditionally been known as a conservative company and a financially prudent one. I would not want to change that image in any way, particularly the financially prudent one. That's a policy that's stood us in good stead both in good times and bad. However I believe as a conglomerate, as a group of companies, there is a lot more we can do in terms of finding ways to create synergy between our group companies. . PARTICIPATING IN INFRASTRUCTURE

With the government's opening up of infrastructure projects we have felt that we would like to participate in key infrastructure projects and be catalysts. Not exactly control them but be catalysts and make them happen so that they in turn positively influence certain developments that we have in key areas. Infrastructure development brings with it a certain amount of risk that traditionally we have not had to deal with. We prefer variables that are within our control. But that having been said, infrastructure is key to the success of many business opportunities in the Philippines.

The fact that we are a comglomerate be it real estate, insurance, food, electronics, a lot of these infrastructure projects affect us in a global way. We can bring that more holistic element to bear on the fact that the projects are important to us, we can perhaps take higher risks than others because it has such positive impact on so many areas that we do business in.

I don't see us moving away from our traditional businesses which have been in banking, insurance, real estate. Those we will continue to grow at a very strong pace, food manufacturing as well. However, we will be moving into new areas -- telecommunications is one major area we are working on right now. We will be in infrastructure, maybe the transportation side in a more visible way. These are all new areas for us that are really very much a cornerstone of the kind of services that are needed in the next century. We as a group would like to keep ourselves entrepreneurial, there will be opportunities that will open up at any point in time given government policies or changes in direction.
POLITICS AND THE AYALAS
What (Defence Secretary Renato) de Villa actually did say is that he considers us a friend. We certainly consider him a friend. That is a far cry from saying he has the support of the Ayalas.

We have been friends for many many years and it looks like he is interested in running for the presidency and we certainly wish him well. He is a person who I think has the kind of value system that the president has inculcated in his administration right now so certainly if he is a successful candidate .. he would certainly make an excellent leader for the country. That having been said we are great believers in widening the kind of choices we have.

Certainly we would be very keen to have someone who has the same kind of philospohy that the president has set -- a free-market type economic policy, a desire to integrate the Philippines more closely to what is happening in ASEAN and the world. Those basic philosophies have stood us in very good stead. I would sincerely hope that whoever replaces him, whoever runs for office, would follow similar policies in the way they look at the presidency.
THE AYALA FAMILY

There is a great deal of pride we have as a family with respect to our association with Ayala. It has gone through many interesting times, it has been associated historically with a lot that has happened in the Philippines through key periods in our history. We are very much a part of the Philippines and certainly our family is very attached and proud of our association with Ayala. That responsibility that we have over the company and maintaining it for future generations is something that both my father and I hold very dear and consider very important.

We see ourselves not just as a profit centre that is good for investments. We see ourselves as a company with a strong value system, as a company with a strong social development component and really a company that believes in doing things with a strong ethical standard. These value systems I believe are really my responsibility to continue .. and keep very much as a part of the way we do business as we grow and as we change in structure and become more aggressive from a corporate point of view.

Certainly I would hope the family continues (in the business) and whether it's my children, my brother's or my sister's, it's only something that we can hope for, but one never knows what the future will bring. But certainly I think the family does believe that it has a responsibility to the company's destiny. We would like to keep that as much as we can over the long-term.
(The opinions expressed in this column represent Mr Ayala's views. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters)
